copyright: Old town and Vltava River, Prague, Czechia (© Lara_Uhryn/Getty Images)
description: This autumnal view from Letná Park looks out over Prague, which grew up along the banks of the Vltava River in Czechia. In today's image, the river winds its way through the historic Old Town and Malá Strana districts, beneath Mánes Bridge in the foreground. Many beautiful bridges now span the Vltava, but for centuries there was only one, Charles Bridge, pictured second from the bottom. Its first stones were laid in 1357 during the reign of Charles IV and until 1841, it was the only way to cross the river on foot. Today its stone arches, gothic towers and statues lining the bridge draw large crowds, so tourists are advised to get there by dawn for the best photographs. Or they could walk on to the next crossing, Legion Bridge, which is less crowded and offers beautiful views of the National Theatre, Prague Castle and its busier neighbour.

copyright: Butte at sunset, Face Canyon, Lake Powell, Utah, USA (© Jeff Foott/Minden)
description: Hidden within an ancient sandstone landscape, Face Canyon is one of 96 canyons stretching out from Lake Powell in southern Utah. Many are far from roads and would be hard to reach if they hadn't been flooded by the lake, created in 1963 during the construction of the Glen Canyon Dam. The lake's waters back up about 300 kilometres, along creeks and canyons which you can explore by boat, kayak or personal watercraft.

copyright: Rainbow Falls on the Wailuku River, Hilo, Hawaii, USA (© Peter Unger/Getty Images)
description: Water, sunlight and lush greenery come together at Rainbow Falls in Hilo, on Hawaii's Big Island. Here, the Wailuku River plunges 24 metres over a lava ledge, sending mist into the air as it reaches the pool below. On sunny mornings, that mist can catch the light and produce the colourful rainbows that gave the falls their name. Known in Hawaiian as Waiānuenue, meaning 'rainbow water', this striking waterfall is surrounded by tropical vegetation and has a special place in Hawaiian legend.

copyright: Sunset Point, Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah, USA (© Colin D. Young/Alamy)
description: Snow transforms Bryce Canyon National Park, blanketing the landscape in white while its fiery orange-red hoodoos rise above the snowy terrain. Seen from Sunset Point, one of the park's most famous overlooks, these fantastical shapes are part of the Claron Formation, whose limestone was deposited about 50 million years ago and later shaped by weathering and erosion. Because much of the park rises above 2,400 metres, snow can arrive as early as October. In today's image, snow clings to the canyon's ridges and spires while mist drifts across the cliffs, creating an iconic winter scene in the American Southwest.

copyright: Red squirrel in Cairngorms National Park, Highlands, Scotland (© Scotland: The Big Picture/Minden Pictures)
description: As Britain's only native squirrel species, red squirrels thrive in Scotland's Cairngorms National Park. An important refuge, the park offers ancient Caledonian pine forests and newer conifer woodlands, with plentiful habitat and food for squirrels foraging for Scots pine seeds, nuts and other tasty morsels year-round. In today's image, a red squirrel is perched amid warm orange and yellow leaves, looking right at home as it ponders its next move in the Scottish Highlands.

Today's image shows the gradual coiling of a young fiddlehead's tip, echoing the geometric patterns seen throughout nature. In maths, the Fibonacci sequence follows a similar progression, each number formed by adding the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and so on. Today is Fibonacci Day, chosen for the numbers of the date (11/23) to honour the sequence. Eventually the young fern frond shown here will unfurl as it grows, but elsewhere in the plant world, the sequence will continue to appear in the spiralling arrangements of sunflower heads, pinecones, succulents and pineapples.

copyright: The chapel and hermitage of Santa Justa in Cantabria, Spain (© Tramont_ana/Getty Images)
description: Tucked into the cliffs of northern Spain's rugged coastline, the 16th-century Hermitage of Santa Justa, seen in today's image, overlooks the crashing waves of the Cantabrian Sea. Built partly into the rock and associated with relics of Saints Justa and Rufina, the small chapel eventually became a pilgrimage site, its sheltered stone walls creating a remarkable contrast with the powerful waves and rocky cliffs surrounding it.
